title: Cache Stampede Prevention with Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch)
subtitle: Mitigating Thundering Herd via Optimal Probabilistic Recomputation vs Mutex Locks
problem_statement: An e-commerce product catalog caches hot inventory data in Redis with a 10-minute TTL. At peak traffic (5,000 RPS), the TTL of the top 5 product keys expires simultaneously. Thousands of concurrent requests experience cache misses and simultaneously hammer PostgreSQL, causing connection pool exhaustion and a cascading outage.

faded_bug.description: Synchronous cache miss fallback allows thundering herd to bypass cache simultaneously upon key expiration.

invariants.description: Cache must implement probabilistic early refresh or mutex lock to prevent database saturation.

probing_ladder.stage_1_validation: Explain the exact sequence of events when a cached item's TTL expires at 12:00:00.000 while 2,000 requests are in flight.
probing_ladder.stage_2_tightening: We have 100,000 keys. If we use distributed locks in Redis (SETNX) to guard recomputation, what happens if the holder process pauses for 800ms during GC?
probing_ladder.stage_3_adversarial: A flash sale starts. 50,000 users query the exact same newly added product which is NOT yet in the cache. How does your solution handle cold-start stampede?
probing_ladder.stage_4_squeeze: We cannot afford an in-memory Redis cluster with replica auto-failover. How can we achieve stampede resilience using local JVM memory only?

counter_probes.counter_question: If 5,000 concurrent threads block on a distributed Redis lock waiting for one worker to compute, what happens to your application server connection pool and thread queue?
counter_probes.expected_staff_answer: Thread starvation and queue buildup occur. XFetch (probabilistic early expiration) or SingleFlight in-memory mutex avoids blocking readers while recomputation runs asynchronously.
